summary:
RotarApp helps farmers in Colombia's Valle del Cauca plan crop rotations that improve soil health and reduce irrigation without using agrochemicals. It works on mobile devices and the web.

Farmers start by drawing their fields on a satellite map and entering their previous crop, any pests they have observed and their main priorities, whether income, water conservation, soil health or erosion control.

The app uses 23 years of historical climate data to simulate different crop rotations across the field at a 30-meter resolution. It evaluates around 50 possible plans, including rotations with nitrogen-fixing cover crops, and produces a heat map showing which options are most likely to perform best in different areas.

Farmers can compare three strategies, including their current practice, and see the reasoning, supporting evidence, expected benefits and uncertainties behind each recommendation.

RotarApp brings together NASA HLS, NASA POWER, NASADEM and Colombian agricultural data. Its purpose is to give farmers better information for making decisions alongside local agronomists, not to make those decisions for them.
details:
Repository link: https://github.com/santiagovelcasallas/RotarApp

What it does and how it works

1. Field and context

The process begins with farmers outlining their fields on a map. They then provide two pieces of information: what they planted last and which pests they noticed. The list of pests changes according to the crop selected, so farmers only see relevant options.

2. Suitability filter

The app examines the field in 30-meter cells to determine which crops are suitable for each area. It considers official IGAC land-capability classifications, soil pH, soil texture, elevation and temperature requirements. The current model covers 24 crops, including seven legumes that can be used to give the soil a period of recovery.

3. Per-pixel simulator

The simulator estimates how crops respond to local conditions using equations for soil water balance based on FAO-56, canopy development, nitrogen availability without synthetic fertilizers, heat stress and waterlogging in clay soils.

It also accounts for pests and diseases. Disease pressure depends partly on the number of days leaves remain wet, while pest pressure can persist when successive crops belong to the same botanical family.

4. Bayesian calibration

We calibrated the model using 13,434 sugarcane regrowth curves derived from NASA HLS observations collected between 2020 and 2025.

To evaluate its performance, we separated training, validation and test data using spatial blocks of 2 km and different years. We also tested the model in an external region that was completely excluded from calibration.

5. Soil Biological Index (IBS)

We developed the Soil Biological Index to estimate conditions that support biological activity in the soil.

The index focuses on periods between harvest and planting, when the ground is exposed and factors such as crop residues and soil disturbance become especially relevant.

It uses indicators derived from satellite observations. This means it provides an estimate of conditions associated with soil life rather than a direct measurement of soil microorganisms.

6. Decision

Each rotation plan is evaluated under 92 combinations of climate conditions and model parameters. The farmer's priorities determine how the different outcomes are weighted.

The app then calculates the probability that each plan will be the best option for every 30-meter cell. These results appear on a heat map, and areas with similar recommendations can be organized into as many as three management zones.

Validation

We evaluated the simulator using data that had not been included in training.

For identifying periods when soil has little or almost no vegetation cover, the model achieved an AUC-ROC between 0.92 and 0.93, with F1 scores ranging from 0.75 to 0.80.

Performance was lower in a completely unseen region, where the F1 score reached 0.61. Even so, the simulator performed better than a gradient-boosting baseline in that external test.

These limitations are important, so the app communicates them openly rather than presenting its predictions as certainties.

Benefits and impact

RotarApp is designed to help farmers understand how different rotation strategies might perform across their land.

Instead of recommending one crop rotation for an entire farm, it identifies areas where particular crops are better suited to local conditions.

It also makes it possible to compare expected outcomes for irrigation needs, erosion, soil biological conditions and gross income under favorable, typical and dry-year conditions.

By recommending crops from different botanical families, the tool can help interrupt pest cycles. Its proposed rotations also incorporate legume cover crops as a biological source of nitrogen, together with no-till planting, avoiding the need for synthetic nitrogen fertilizers.

Our broader goal is to make agroecological crop rotation easier to plan and evaluate, especially for smallholder farmers who need practical recommendations they can review with a local agronomist.

Creativity

One of the main features of RotarApp is that it does not treat an entire field as if conditions were uniform. Instead, it estimates the probability of different rotations performing best in each 30-meter cell. This allows farmers to consider different strategies within the same field.

Another distinctive element is the Soil Biological Index, which evaluates conditions associated with soil life during the periods when the soil is exposed between crops.

The simulator can also evaluate crops that do not appear in the satellite observations used for calibration. It does this by combining physical equations with parameters calibrated from available data.

Where observations are limited, the model represents that uncertainty rather than assuming its estimates are equally reliable everywhere.

Tools

Model development

The simulator was developed in Python using NumPy, SciPy, pyproj and rasterio. We also used scikit-learn to build the baseline model used for comparison.

Data sources

Satellite observations come from NASA HLS, accessed through Microsoft Planetary Computer. Climate and terrain information comes from NASA POWER and NASADEM.

For soil and land suitability, we use IGAC maps and SoilGrids. Agricultural market prices come from DANE-SIPSA, while our pest database draws on information published by ICA, Cenicaña and Agrosavia.

Application

The mobile and web application uses Expo, React Native and TypeScript. It includes Leaflet and native mapping tools with Esri satellite imagery, connected to a Python API.

The project was developed using a standard laptop, without specialized computing equipment.

Factors we considered

We designed the application with smallholder farmers in mind, including users who may have limited experience with digital tools or difficulty reading complex technical information. This is why the interface prioritizes mobile access and straightforward explanations.

The agricultural approach is based on avoiding agrochemicals, reducing irrigation needs and encouraging practices that support long-term soil health.

We also considered the limitations of the available information. Production costs have not yet been incorporated, so the economic results currently represent gross income rather than net profit.

Another planned improvement is the integration of daily rainfall data from GPM IMERG to better represent extreme rainfall events.

The initial implementation focuses on two pilot zones where the necessary datasets are available.

Finally, the app makes clear that its recommendations should be reviewed under local conditions with an agronomist. The intention is to support informed agricultural decisions while keeping farmers and local experts involved in the process.
